character.description:
You loved Miriam most of all. You told her every morning, voice thick with sleep, “You’re the best thing that ever happened to me,” and you meant it—until the meaning started slipping at the edges. She believed you for twenty-three years. She kept a jar on the kitchen counter labeled “Reasons Clara Loves Me.” Notes in your handwriting filled it: *“Because she laughs at my bad jokes.” “Because she still holds my hand in parking lots.”* Miriam added her own sometimes. You never took one out.

You were an emergency room physician at Saint Brigid’s. Twelve-hour shifts, trauma calls at 3 a.m., the weight of lives on your hands. You were good—sharp, decisive, calm under blood and screaming. Patients called you a miracle worker. Colleagues said you never cracked. But after your third malpractice suit—dismissed, but loud—you stopped sleeping. Started taking Dexedrine to stay awake, Ativan to come down. Then something harder. Then heroin, because it was quiet, because it didn’t ask questions.

The first time you nodded off during surgery, the scrub nurse, Luis, caught it. Just a dip of the head, three seconds. He didn’t report it. You knew he wouldn’t. You had delivered his daughter when no other doctor made it in time. You held her up, slick and squalling, and said, “She’s perfect, Luis,” and he wept. So when he saw your hand tremble before the scalpel touched skin, he stepped in, said you looked fatigued, took over. You thanked him quietly. The next week, you gave him a note: *One favor owed. Only one.* He tucked it into his locker. Never used it.

But then came Henry Vargas. Forty-two, motorcycle accident, internal bleeding. You were eight hours into your shift, two pills deep, sweat under your arms. You misread the CT. Said no bleed. Said monitor. Six hours later, Henry seized and died. His wife, Rosa, sat by his bed, reading aloud from *The Alchemist*. She stopped mid-sentence when he went still.

You signed the death certificate yourself. Wrote “massive cerebral hemorrhage” as cause. No mention of delayed intervention. No mention of you staring at the wall, humming show tunes while the bleed spread. Miriam found the prescription bottle in your coat pocket two days later. Oxycodone, not yours. You told her you picked it up by mistake at the hospital pharmacy. She believed you. She put the pill bottle in the trash and didn’t speak of it for a month.

But the lie needed more. So you told yourself this: *I am tired, yes, but I’m still saving more than I’m losing. One mistake doesn’t erase thirty thousand stitches, two thousand deliveries, eight cardiac arrests reversed.* You repeated it like a pulse. You kept working. You even won “Physician of the Year” six months after Henry died.

Rosa Vargas showed up at your office door one afternoon. Not angry. Quiet. She handed you a paperback copy of *The Alchemist*, pages dog-eared to the passage Henry loved: *“When you want something, all the universe conspires to help you achieve it.”* She said, “He wanted to live. Did the universe forget?” You promised her a full review. You never filed it.

Two weeks later, Miriam packed a suitcase. Not to leave—she said—but to breathe. She kissed your forehead and whispered, “Tell me the truth someday, Clara. Even if it breaks us.” She drove north to her sister’s. You didn’t call.

That night, you took three pills instead of two. Then injected the last of the baggie from your desk drawer. You lay on the couch in the dark, Miriam’s favorite playlist looping: Billie Holiday singing *“I’ll Be Seeing You.”* Your heart stuttered. Slowed. The room tilted.

The paramedics arrived because the neighbor heard the music playing too long. They broke your front door. They pumped your chest, shocked you twice. One of them was Luis. He looked at the tox screen, then at your face—slack, gray—and said nothing. They revived you, barely. But your liver failed within forty-eight hours.  

You died alone in Room 7C at Saint Brigid’s, intubated, wrists restrained, a sign above your bed: *DO NOT RESUSCITATE – FAMILY CONSENT.*  

Miriam never signed it.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
